items.followUp: What is photophosphorylation, and how do cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation differ?

rubric.why: Identifies the two photosystems and the direction of electron movement.
rubric.description: Names photosystem II and photosystem I and states that electrons pass from one to the other.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both photosystems and electron movement from PSII to PSI.

rubric.why: Explains why the pathway is called the Z-scheme and identifies its role in non-cyclic electron flow.
rubric.description: Explains that the electron-energy pattern is Z-shaped during non-cyclic electron transport, which begins with electrons from water and ends with their transfer to NADP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the Z-shaped energy pattern and the non-cyclic pathway endpoints.

modelAnswer: The Z-scheme is the non-cyclic movement of electrons from water through photosystem II and photosystem I to NADP.
The energy-level changes of the electrons during this pathway form a pattern resembling the letter Z.

items.followUp: Describe how water moves from the roots to the leaves through the xylem.

rubric.why: Shows the different materials used and produced in photosynthesis and respiration.
rubric.description: Gives a correct difference in reactants and products.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen, whereas respiration uses glucose and oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water.

rubric.why: Shows a second valid difference, such as location or energy change.
rubric.description: Gives another correct difference between the processes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a paired distinction, for example photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts and stores light energy in glucose, while respiration occurs mainly in mitochondria and releases energy.

modelAnswer: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts and uses carbon dioxide, water and light energy to make glucose and oxygen; respiration occurs mainly in mitochondria and breaks down glucose using oxygen.
Photosynthesis stores light energy in glucose, whereas respiration releases energy from glucose.

items.followUp: Name two sources of dietary fibre and state one benefit of fibre in the diet.

rubric.why: Identifies dietary fibre as indigestible material from plants.
rubric.description: Defines dietary fibre.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is indigestible plant material, such as cellulose.

rubric.why: States a key role of fibre in the digestive system.
rubric.description: Gives a function of dietary fibre.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that fibre helps bowel movement or prevents constipation.

modelAnswer: Dietary fibre is the indigestible part of plant food, such as cellulose.
It adds bulk to food and helps its movement through the intestine, preventing constipation.

items.followUp: Explain how evaporation from leaves causes water to rise in xylem vessels.

rubric.why: Identifies water loss from leaves as the starting event.
rubric.description: Links transpiration to evaporation of water from the leaves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that evaporation or transpiration from leaves initiates the pull.

rubric.why: Describes the resulting upward pull through the xylem.
rubric.description: Explains that the pull draws water upward through the xylem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that tension pulls the continuous water column upward in xylem vessels.

modelAnswer: Transpiration pull is the force that draws water upward through the xylem of a plant.
Evaporation of water from leaf surfaces creates tension, which pulls the continuous column of water up from the roots.

items.followUp: Trace the path of blood in systemic circulation, naming the chambers and major blood vessels involved.

rubric.why: Identifies the route carrying blood from the heart to the lungs.
rubric.description: States that blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery and goes to the lungs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct heart-to-lungs route.

rubric.why: Identifies the return route of oxygenated blood to the heart.
rubric.description: States that blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct lungs-to-heart return route.

modelAnswer: Pulmonary circulation is the circulation of blood from the right ventricle of the heart to the lungs and back to the heart.
Blood travels to the lungs through the pulmonary artery and returns to the left atrium through the pulmonary veins.

items.followUp: Define any four branches of biology, other than the ones in your answer.

rubric.why: Recognises branches of biology and gives their subject areas.
rubric.description: Correctly defines two branches of biology.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for two accurate branch definitions; accept 1 mark for each.

rubric.why: Completes the requested five definitions with accurate subject areas.
rubric.description: Correctly defines three additional branches, for five definitions in total.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for three further accurate definitions; accept other standard branches with correct definitions. The total for five definitions is capped at 4 marks.

modelAnswer: Zoology is the branch of biology that deals with animals.
Botany is the branch of biology that deals with plants.
Microbiology is the branch of biology that studies microorganisms.
Genetics is the branch of biology that studies inheritance and variation.
Ecology is the branch of biology that studies organisms and their relationships with one another and their environment.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and function of the cell membrane.

rubric.why: Identifies the cell wall as the outer covering of a plant cell and its principal material.
rubric.description: States the position and main composition of the cell wall.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as an outer covering of plant cells made chiefly of cellulose.

rubric.why: Describes the layer that joins neighbouring plant cells.
rubric.description: Describes the middle lamella.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the middle lamella, rich in pectin, cements adjacent cells together.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the primary wall by its thin, flexible nature.
rubric.description: Describes the primary cell wall.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the primary wall is thin and flexible and forms while the cell is growing.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the secondary wall by its position and thickness.
rubric.description: Describes the secondary cell wall.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the secondary wall is deposited inside the primary wall and is thicker.

rubric.why: Includes a key structural material or property of the wall.
rubric.description: States a further structural feature or property of the cell wall.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct detail such as lignin strengthening some walls or the wall being freely permeable.

modelAnswer: The cell wall is a rigid, non-living outer covering of a plant cell, situated outside the cell membrane.
It is made chiefly of cellulose and is freely permeable.
The middle lamella, rich in pectin, joins neighbouring cells together.
The primary wall is thin and flexible and forms while the cell is growing.
A thicker secondary wall may be deposited inside the primary wall; it may contain lignin, which adds strength.

items.followUp: Explain the lock-and-key model of enzyme action and state what happens to the enzyme after the reaction.

rubric.why: Identifies where the substrate binds to the enzyme.
rubric.description: States that the substrate binds at the enzyme's active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the active site as the substrate-binding region.

rubric.why: Explains the specific fit between enzyme and substrate.
rubric.description: Explains the lock-and-key fit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substrate has a shape complementary to the enzyme's active site.

rubric.why: Names the temporary intermediate formed during the reaction.
rubric.description: States that an enzyme-substrate complex forms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the temporary enzyme-substrate complex.

rubric.why: Explains the outcome of the reaction and why the enzyme can act again.
rubric.description: States that products are released and the enzyme remains unchanged or reusable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that products are released and the enzyme is unchanged and can be reused.

modelAnswer: The substrate binds to the enzyme's active site, whose shape is complementary to the substrate, like a key fitting a lock.
A temporary enzyme-substrate complex forms.
The enzyme converts the substrate into product or products, which are then released.
The enzyme remains unchanged and can be used again.
